intro_html: Dublin coddle is a working-class dish with no pretensions whatsoever. Sausages, bacon, onions, and potatoes go into a pot, broth goes over the top, and the lid goes on. That is the recipe. It got its name because the ingredients coddle, meaning they sit in barely simmering liquid until everything softens and the flavors trade places. There is no browning ritual and no fancy technique, and it comes out tasting like somebody's grandmother made it. This is also one of those rare dishes that is genuinely better reheated, because the potatoes keep absorbing the sausage fat overnight.
cost_closing_html: About $1.53 a bowl for a pot of sausage, bacon, and potatoes that could feed a construction crew.
shop_smart: Potatoes are the cheapest calorie in the store and they are the backbone here. Buy the big bag, not the loose ones, and keep them somewhere dark so they do not sprout.
Bratwurst stands in for Irish bangers without apology. Bangers are hard to find and cost a premium when you do. Brats are the same idea, always stocked, and often on sale.
Buy bacon in the two-pound pack when it goes on sale. It freezes fine, and half of it goes to breakfast for the rest of the week.
Skip the browning step and you skip a pan. The traditional method really does just layer everything raw, which means one pot to wash.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cut the bacon into thick pieces and cook it in a large dutch oven until it renders and crisps at the edges.
Cut the bratwurst into thick chunks and brown them lightly in the bacon fat, which is optional in the traditional version but adds a lot.
Add the sliced yellow onions and garlic and cook until they soften and pick up the fat.
Peel the potatoes and cut them into large chunks, then layer them over the meat and onions.
Pour in the chicken broth so it comes about two thirds of the way up, and season with salt, black pepper, dried thyme, and dried parsley.
Cover and cook low, either on the stovetop or in a moderate oven, until the potatoes are completely tender and the broth has turned cloudy and rich.
Uncover for the last stretch if you want the top layer to color, then taste and adjust the salt.
portion_html: Put the full pot on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight from Step 1, and divide by 14. Scoop that weight into each container, making sure every one gets sausage, bacon, and potato rather than all broth. Every serving lands near 773 calories with 38 grams of protein. It thickens as it cools, which is exactly what you want.

steps: Cut and render the bacon in a large dutch oven until crisp at the edges.
Brown the bratwurst chunks in the bacon fat.
Add sliced onions and garlic and cook until softened.
Layer large potato chunks over the meat and pour in the broth.
Season, cover, and cook low until the potatoes are completely tender.
Adjust salt and portion into 14 containers.
